items.title: 27.3.2 Role of Inhibitors in Enzyme-Catalysed Reactions

source_refs.note: Topic 27.3.2 with the cobra box and the first Quick Check 27.3, answered (PDF 168-169); Figures 27.8 and 27.9 are redrawn in the topic 27.3 figure. Printed slips are corrected in a warning; the book's equating of non-competitive with irreversible is reported as the book's. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Small molecules or ions that cause enzymes to lose their catalytic activity are inhibitors. Different inhibitors act differently, but all stop the active site from binding the substrate.

items: Competitive (reversible) inhibitors have the same shape as the substrate. The substrate and the inhibitor compete for the active site; the more inhibitor, the more the enzyme is deactivated for its substrate. For example, butanedioate (succinate, -OOC-CH2-CH2-COO-) is oxidised by the enzyme dehydrogenase succinate, and propanedioate (malonate, -OOC-CH2-COO-) inhibits this enzyme because it resembles succinate.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The enzyme's name is succinate dehydrogenase.

blocks.alt: Left: an enzyme with an active site and a substrate S moving towards it. An inhibitor I with a similar shape is added, and an arrow leads to the enzyme-inhibitor complex: the inhibitor sits in the active site, held by a non-covalent bond, and the substrate S is left outside.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.8: Action of reversible inhibitor (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.8; the bond label is corrected).
blocks.long_description: The printed figure labels the inhibitor's attachment 'Covalent Bond'; a reversible inhibitor binds by weak non-covalent forces, so the label reads non-covalent bond.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 27.8 labels the reversible inhibitor's attachment 'Covalent Bond'; a reversible (competitive) inhibitor is held by non-covalent bonds, as labelled above.

items: Non-competitive (irreversible) inhibitors are small ions or molecules that change the shape of the active site so that it is no longer available to the substrate. An enzyme to which an irreversible inhibitor, such as a poison, an antibiotic, an anti-metabolite or some drugs, is attached loses its activity permanently; such inhibition can cause severe health problems or even death. Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor of the enzyme transpeptidase, which bacteria need to build their cell walls. Thus insulin kills bacteria by disrupting the cell wall enzyme.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: It is penicillin, not insulin, that kills bacteria by blocking the cell-wall enzyme transpeptidase.

blocks.alt: Two yellow enzymes. In the first, the green substrate fits its active site. In the second, a red non-competitive inhibitor is bound at another site on the side of the enzyme; the active site has changed shape and the substrate no longer fits.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.9: Action of non-competitive inhibitor (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.9).

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Cobra venom contains the enzyme PLA2, which can break down the membranes of red blood cells, causing haemolysis, swelling of the affected organ and ultimately death.
